items.title: Investigation: conda-forge scikit-learn slower than PyPI (ExtraTrees case)
items.body:
While looking at [builds comparison results](https://probabl-ai.github.io/scikit-learn-benchmarks/builds_comparison.html) from my benchmarks (https://github.com/probabl-ai/scikit-learn-benchmarks), I noticed `ExtraTrees*.fit` was often ~25% slower on conda-forge builds of
scikit-learn 1.9.0 than on PyPI wheels.

Two distinct bugs were found along the way; only the second one explains the slowdown:

1. **O3 vs O2** (documented in #34865): `-O3` in meson doesn't survive an environment `CFLAGS` that also sets `-O2` (which conda-forge's compiler activation does).

2. **Version of `glibc`** (cause of the slowdown): conda-forge compiles scikit-learn against a `sysroot_linux-64=2.17` (glibc 2.17, from 2012-12-25). That old glibc's `<math.h>` defines the `isnan()` macro as a dispatch to glibc-internal `__isnanf`/`__isnan` functions instead of `__builtin_isnan*`. GCC can't recognize or inline those, so `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx`'s `isnan(value)` calls — sitting in the hottest loop of tree-building (`find_min_max`, `partition_samples`) — become genuine non-inlined function calls. This is `fit`-specific (confirmed: `predict`, which doesn't call these functions, shows no slowdown) and fully reproduced from source once the exact sysroot was pinned.


This is very likely **not scikit-learn-specific**: any conda-forge package with a hot-loop `isnan()`/`isinf()` call is plausibly exposed the same way.

~~=> TODO: Open an issue in conda-forge~~ Done: I posted a comment here: https://github.com/conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock/issues/108

### Proposed fix

Replace `from libc.math cimport isnan` / `isnan(value)` in `sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` (and any other tree/HGB hot loop doing the same) with the self-inequality NaN test `value != value`. Pure comparison, nothing to inline, immune to this class of bug on any compiler/libc, forever.

### Root cause, in detail

*(pure LLM write-up)*

<details>

`sklearn/tree/_partitioner.pyx` (`DensePartitioner.find_min_max`, `.partition_samples`) and `sklearn/tree/_utils.pxd` call `isnan(value)` on `float32_t` data, via `from libc.math cimport isnan`. This runs once per sample per feature scan during `fit`; never during `predict`.

The feedstock's CI pin file (`.ci_support/linux_64_python3.12.____cpython.yaml` at the 1.9.0 release commit) sets `c_stdlib: sysroot`, `c_stdlib_version: '2.17'`. That sysroot's `math.h` has:

```c
#  define isnan(x) \
     (sizeof (x) == sizeof (float) ? __isnanf (x) \
      : sizeof (x) == sizeof (double) ? __isnan (x) : __isnanl (x))
```

Once the preprocessor expands this, the identifier `isnan` is gone from
the translation unit — GCC has nothing left to recognize as a builtin, so
`__isnanf` (an ordinary external glibc symbol, not a compiler intrinsic)
gets a real out-of-line call. Modern glibc instead defines `isnan(x)` as
`__builtin_isnan(x)` directly, which GCC folds to 2 instructions
(`ucomiss`/`setp`). PyPI/manylinux wheels don't hit this because they're
built with devtoolset-style toolchains: modern compiler *and* modern
headers, achieving old-system compatibility via glibc *symbol versioning*
at link time rather than by literally compiling against old headers.

Confirmed end to end:
- `perf`-profiled real installed PyPI vs conda-forge packages
  (`ExtraTreesRegressor.fit`, `n_features=30`): conda-forge spends 12.6% of
  samples in `__isnanf` alone; PyPI doesn't show it in the top 15 at all.
- Disassembled both real `.so` files directly: conda-forge's
  `find_min_max` has `call *0x1791f(%rip)  # <__isnanf@GLIBC_2.2.5>`;
  PyPI's has no call at all.
- Reproduced from source: rebuilding the actual v1.9.0 tag with the exact
  matching GCC (14.3.0-19, confirmed via the real binary's own
  `.comment` section) reproduced nothing *until* `sysroot_linux-64=2.17`
  was pinned explicitly (every environment had otherwise resolved the
  latest default, 2.39) — at which point the non-inlined call and the
  larger function size reappeared byte-for-byte.
- Same `isnan()` call pattern, same functions, confirmed still present on
  current `main` (the categorical-feature/Breiman-shortcut work added
  since 1.9.0 didn't touch this code path — `find_min_max` compiles to the
  identical byte size on both).

</details>

### Everything else that was tried and ruled out

Before finding the sysroot, a long list of variables was controlled for one at a time and **did not** reproduce the real-world gap when rebuilding from source with the real conda-forge `gcc_linux-64`/`gxx_linux-64` toolchain:

<details>

- `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (~1.7% effect — this is the Meson bug above)
- `-march=nocona -mtune=haswell` vs no override
- GCC version: 16.2.0, 13.4.0, and the exact `14.3.0-19` patch build
  (pinning `gcc_impl_linux-64`/`gxx_impl_linux-64`/`binutils_impl_linux-64`
  precisely, since `gcc_impl_linux-64` has its own build-number sequence
  independent of the `gcc_linux-64` wrapper)
- Cython version (real binary uses 3.2.5; early rebuilds had picked up
  3.3.0 by default — controlled for, no effect)
- Exact v1.9.0 source tag vs current `main`
- Editable install vs literal `python -m build -w` wheel build (matching
  `build.sh` exactly)
- `-fno-merge-constants` (the extra flag conda-forge adds under
  `CONDA_BUILD=1`)
- joblib version, core-count detection, BLAS threading config — all
  identical between real PyPI and conda-forge installs

</details>

### Interest in fixing the bug

Yes, I'll open the PR very soon.

items.title: Investigation: Meson silently downgrades -O3 to -O2 under conda-forge CFLAGS

labels.name: Needs Benchmarks
labels.description: A tag for the issues and PRs which require some benchmarks

items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Meson's `buildtype: release` implies `-O3` for every compiled extension in the project. Under conda-forge, it doesn't: conda-forge's compiler activation injects its own `-O2` via `CFLAGS`/`CXXFLAGS`, and Meson appends environment flags *after* its own optimization flag on the compiler command line. GCC/Clang use the **last** `-O` flag, so conda-forge's `-O2` silently wins:
```
cc ... -O3 ... -march=nocona -mtune=haswell ... -O2 -ffunction-sections -pipe ... -c foo.c
```



This was first noticed via `sklearn/tree/meson.build`'s `override_options: ['optimization=3']` (an explicit ask that's supposed to matter for `_splitter.pyx`/`_partitioner.pyx`'s branch-heavy loops) silently doing nothing under conda-forge, but that's just the one place the override was visible enough to check.

This is a known Meson/conda-forge interaction, not new: mesonbuild/meson#15055 (closed as docs — "CFLAGS in general tend to override buildtype flags, as they are appended") and conda-forge/ctng-compiler-activation-feedstock#157 (still open/unmerged for gcc/Linux).

**However: benchmarking `-O2` vs `-O3` in isolation (real conda-forge toolchain) did not show any observable performance effect on what I tried for now.**. Contrary to an other conda-forge compilation chain setting that does cause an important slowdown on `ExtraTrees*`, see: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34869

For now, I'm not sure we should bother fixing it. Claude had a way to fix it, see PR #34864 (but I closed it for now).

items.title: CI Align wheel workflow in `scikit-learn` and `scikit-learn-release` repos
items.body:
> [!WARNING]
> This issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our [contributing guidelines](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html), and in particular the sections for [new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors) and the ["Needs triage"](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#issues-tagged-needs-triage) label.

Looking at numpy approach, the idea would be to have `scikit-learn` `wheels.yml` be a "simplified" version of `scikit-learn-release` `wheels.yml` so that we can catch most wheels error in the `scikit-learn` repo. numpy went for one wheels build per platform with the minimal Python version.

There are at least to things:
- [ ] use cibuildwheel directly + remove the Docker set-up since the minimal Docker image is tested in scikit-learn-release. This would allow to get rid of the intermittent Docker on Windows GHA issue: https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34569. There are other things to sync, like bash scripts and config (maybe it would be better if both repos use a `pyroject.toml` or a `cibuildwheel.toml`, rather than `cibuildwheel.toml` for scikit-learn-release and `pyproject.toml`)
- [ ] which wheels build do we want to run in `scikit-learn` and on which trigger. Do we want to do something like numpy, i.e. one wheels build per platform for the minimal Python version? Do we want to keep `[cd build]` to test wheels only on demand? See [numpy PR](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/29540) for numpy and [scipy PR](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/24536) for more details.

First item can be work on already. Second one may need a bit of discussion.

Caveat:
- our lock-files setup gives us confidence that a new release of our dependencies will not break all PRs at once. What do we want to do about this if we start having wheels build on each PR push, hope that it doesn't happen this often? Last time it happened was with cython see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/34525. In principle we should have caught it in the scipy-dev build and reported it earlier to cython but we didn't 🤷. An alternative is to have lock files in wheels build, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/issues/1, but that seems to be further away in the future IMO.

To think about for the future:
- how do we make sure that both `wheels.yml` does not diverge too much. AFAICT numpy has not a ready-made solution but they introduced this check https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/30166 to make sure that the pinned scipy-openblas version is the same in both repos.
- automatic wheels failure issue creation, see https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release/issues/6

items.title: CI Add bot comment when linting job fails early
items.body:
Seen in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/34676#issuecomment-5249089742. The linting fails early so there is no `linting_output.txt` from the linting workflow.

The bot comment workflow then fails [build log](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/actions/runs/31459117010/job/93678907739)

That means there is no bot comment indicating there is a linting issue ...

Probably the simplest thing to do when there is no `linting_output.txt` is to say click "Update branch" or run a command like `git pull upstream main --no-rebase` which should get rid of the error.

cc @AnneBeyer if you are interested 😉.

items.title: Path to moving from hosting the site scikit-learn/scikit-learn.github.io to cloudflare
items.body:
This is the plan to get `scikit-learn.org` hosted on Cloudflare

### Requirements
1. `scikit-learn.org`'s website is on Cloudflare.
2. The versioned docs continue to live in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn.github.io.
3. The `dev` website lives in Cloudflare and does not get pushed to https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn.github.io.

### Implementation path
1. Update https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/build_tools/circle/list_versions.py so the `zip` and `pdf` files point to Github. (A future extension is to upload `zip` and `pdf` to Cloudflare R2)
2. Manually deploy current website to Cloudflare.

items.title: Support for building against a SciPy which uses ILP64 BLAS and `cython_blas`
items.body:
Hi all, this issue is to propose adding support for building scikit-learn against a SciPy install that was built with ILP64 (i.e., 64-bit integers rather than the default LP64 / 32-bit integers - see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64-bit_computing#64-bit_data_models). 

### Context

SciPy has wanted to have solid/full ILP64  support for years (efforts going back to 2020, and feature requests before that), because there are use cases and algorithms where support for large arrays where array indices don't fit in plain `int`'s is desirable. In the next SciPy release, 1.18.0, this will finally be arriving.

When building from source, there will actually be three builld modes:
1. LP64-only (default)
2. ILP64-only (opt-in with `-Duse-ilp64=true`)
3. ILP64 for all SciPy internals, but LP64 for `linalg.blas` and `linalg.cython_blas` low-level interfaces  (opt-in with `-Duse-ilp64=true -Dcython-blas-abi=lp64`)

See https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/building/blas_lapack.html#bit-integer-ilp64-blas-lapack for details.

Wheels on PyPI will continue to be LP64-only, so the ABI of `cython_blas` and `cython_lapack` won't be broken. However, when building from source, ILP64 can be chosen - and going ILP64-only means that downstream users of `scipy.linalg.blas|lapack|cython_blas|cython_lapack` need to work with that change.

Mode (3) can be useful as a transition mechanism for adopters (and wouldn't affect scikit-learn), but mode (2) is probably preferred. 

### Proposed solution

It is possible for scikit-learn and other downstream users to detect how SciPy was built, and adapt automatically - no new build flag will be needed in scikit-learn, it should "just work". Essentially, `scipy.linalg.cython_blas` will expose a `blas_int` that can be used. It's also not too difficult to use that conditionally when it exists, and fall back to plain `int` otherwise.

Then, there are two ways scikit-learn can go for its own Cython code:

1. Handle the change in [sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx) with a small shim in each function, and keep [sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd) unchanged.
2. Change `_cython_blas.pxd` as well to use `blas_int`, meaning all consumers of that interface (~15 files currently) need to be adapted as well.

It's not an either/or. Option 1 is a very localized change, and should probably be done either way. Option 2 can always be done later - it has the benefit of actually enabling use of large arrays with scikit-learn APIs as well (option 1 doesn't, because `_cython_blas.pxd` still uses `int`). So it depends on whether there's a benefit in doing that.

### Next step

I plan to open a PR for (1) soon. This is fairly well-tested now (https://github.com/rgommers/pixi-sklearn-ilp64), and we are adding a test package to SciPy CI that closely mirrors scikit-learn's `_cython_blas` wrappers. Also, we now have a regression test for Cython ABI/signature changes, so that should be fine now.

If you prefer to do (2), I'd be happy to work on that as well.

items.title: Use clang-cl (LLVM) compiler for Windows ARM64 wheel builds
items.body:
### Describe the workflow you want to enable

Scikit-learn currently ships ARM64 Windows wheels built with MSVC. This proposal is to switch the Windows ARM64 wheel build to use **clang-cl** in the CI pipeline for improved performance and build reliability.

 **Initial scikit-learn implementation already exists** 
  A working PR switching the win_arm64 CI wheel build to clang-cl was raised and demonstrates the change builds and passes tests successfully. 
   [scikit-learn PR #33435](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33435)

**Motivation:**

The need for clang-cl on Windows ARM64 is well documented across the ecosystem:

 **CPython acknowledged the ARM64 Windows performance gap** 
  Python release binaries on ARM64 Windows show significantly lower performance compared to x64, traced to MSVC's weaker ARM64  auto-vectorisation. This is the upstream root cause that affects all Python packages built with MSVC on this platform.
  [python/cpython #134524](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/134524)
 
 **Community discussion on clang-cl for Windows ARM64** 
  A dedicated thread on Python.org Ideas discusses using clang-cl to address the performance gap in Windows ARM64 Python packages, with broad agreement from the scientific Python community that LLVM is the right path forward for this platform.
   [Python.org Discussions](https://discuss.python.org/t/using-clang-cl-for-better-performance-on-windows-on-arm/)

  **NumPy formally proposed and adopted clang-cl for win_arm64** 
  NumPy raised this as an enhancement issue to provide Windows ARM64 wheels compiled with the LLVM toolchain, citing the same MSVC  ARM64 vectorisation gap. This was subsequently implemented and NumPy now ships win_arm64 wheels built with clang-cl.
    [numpy/numpy #29174](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/29174)
    [numpy/numpy #28106](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/issues/28106)
    [numpy/numpy PR #28246](https://github.com/numpy/numpy/pull/28246) 

NumPy and SciPy 
scikit-learn's two core dependencies already ship win_arm64 wheelsbuilt with clang-cl.


### Describe your proposed solution

Switch the `win_arm64` CI wheel build from MSVC to **clang-cl** (LLVM). The change is scoped to Windows ARM64 only all other platforms (win_amd64, Linux, macOS) remain unchanged.

**Test suite**

All scikit-learn tests pass with the clang-cl build. The implementation includes a fix for a `uint32_t` redefinition that 
occurs specifically with clang-cl on Windows.

### Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

items.title: CI Add aggregating job in GHA to summarize statuses of all unit test jobs and be used a required check
items.body: Follow-up on https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/32434, the idea would be to have a single ggregating job (green if all unit test jobs are green, red if one of the unit test is red) to use it as required checks. Azure had a built-in aggregated job which we were using for our required check and right now our GHA required checks are based on a number of exact job names which is a bit brittle. From a quick look some time ago https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31832#issuecomment-3116678817: - [github.com/orgs/community/discussions/4324#discussioncomment-13335158](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/4324#discussioncomment-13335158) - third-party GitHub action [re-actors/alls-green](https://github.com/re-actors/alls-green?rgh-link-date=2025-07-25T07%3A08%3A55Z) that seems to handle this use case I am wondering whether if this is doable/easy to take into account the status "optional" jobs, for example free-threaded or scipy-dev in a PR. ---------------- More details, GitHub required checks are managed centrally via the web UI on a job level and are based on exact job names. Setting is [here](https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/settings/branch_protection_rules/23621449) That means that it you change a job name in `main` and then update the required checks, all the PRs will have a pending job that never complete and the PR can not be merged. The work-around is to merge `main` into your PR branch. Having a single aggregating job used a I think @FrancoisPgm had an initial look at one point, feel free to add more relevant context if you have some.

items.title: Potential improvements for changelog/website situation during RC -> final transition
items.body:
So it's quite confusing and I don't know how easy/hard this is to improve the situation, it mostly looks like this is an unintended side-effect of our release process + towncrier setup. Since this is a 2-week transition period, nobody has yet found the time to figure out what possible improvements we could do.

Previously mentioned in https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/issues/32807 and https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/31469#issuecomment-2931890657 and probably other places.

Let's try to summarize the issues:
- the changelog is not easily findable on the website. stable or dev website "ongoing development scikit-learn changelog 1.8" (bottom left) both point to https://scikit-learn.org/dev/whats_new/v1.8.html#version-1-8-0 which is empty. This is probably the easiest thing for now: copy the 1.8 changelog from `1.8.X` branch to `main` so that the 1.8 changelog is correct on the `dev` website.
- towncrier setup: during the rc -> final period, we still have the fragments in doc/whats_new/upcoming changes in both `main` and `1.8.X`. For the final, we generate the changelog with towncrier (without `--keep`), which removes the fragments. Then we forward-port this change in `main`. IIRC this was taken from another project, for example [astropy does that](https://docs.astropy.org/en/latest/development/maintainers/releasing.html#rendering-the-changelog) as well.
- slightly annoying but less crucial: during the transition period, the 1.9 changelog on dev website has all the changes that will go in 1.8 plus some that will go in 1.9 

cc @jeremiedbb in case you remember if you put more info about the situation somewhere.

> [!WARNING]
> This is not a good first issue to contribute. Great if you are interested to contribute to scikit-learn 🙏. Please have a look at our [contributing doc](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html) and in particular the section [Issues for new contributors](https://scikit-learn.org/dev/developers/contributing.html#new-contributors).
